title: Fluids at Rest
description: Pressure, buoyancy, and why ships float

concepts.title: Pressure
concepts.contentHtml:
Pressure is force per unit area: P = F/A. Measured in pascals (Pa = N/m²). Atmospheric pressure at sea level is about 10⁵ Pa.

In a static fluid, pressure increases with depth: P = P₀ + ρgh. Each meter of water adds about 10⁴ Pa — roughly a tenth of an atmosphere.

The shape of the container doesn't matter; only depth does. This is sometimes counterintuitive — a thin column and a wide pool at the same depth have the same pressure at the bottom.

concepts.title: Pascal's Principle & Hydraulics
concepts.contentHtml:
Pascal's principle: a pressure change applied to a confined fluid is transmitted undiminished throughout.

This is the basis of hydraulic systems. Push down on a small piston with force F₁ over area A₁; the pressure P = F₁/A₁ acts on a larger piston of area A₂, producing force F₂ = P · A₂. A small effort, multiplied by the area ratio, lifts a car.

Energy is conserved — the small piston travels much further than the big one moves.

concepts.title: Archimedes' Principle
concepts.contentHtml:
The buoyant force on a submerged object equals the weight of the fluid it displaces. So an object floats if its average density is less than the fluid's, sinks otherwise.

A steel ship floats because its hull encloses enough air that the ship's average density is below water. A submarine takes on or expels water in ballast tanks to change its average density and dive or surface.

This principle saved Archimedes from the bathtub — and the king's gold.

title: Fluids in Motion — Bernoulli & Continuity
description: Why airplanes fly and balls curve

concepts.title: Continuity Equation
concepts.contentHtml:
For an incompressible fluid in steady flow, mass conservation gives the continuity equation: ρ A v = constant along a streamline. Density factor cancels for water; cross-section times velocity is constant.

Pinch a garden hose; the water speeds up. Same flow rate, smaller area means higher velocity. Rivers narrow and rapid versus broad and slow are continuity in action.

concepts.title: Bernoulli's Equation
concepts.contentHtml:
For an inviscid, incompressible, steady flow along a streamline, energy conservation gives Bernoulli's equation:

P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant.

Sum of pressure, kinetic energy density, and gravitational potential energy density is constant along a streamline. Faster flow → lower pressure (the kinetic term grew, so the static term shrank).

concepts.title: Lift & the Magnus Effect
concepts.contentHtml:
An airfoil deflects air downward. By Newton's third law, the air pushes the wing upward — that's lift.

Bernoulli's equation gives a partial picture: faster flow over the curved upper surface means lower pressure there, contributing to lift. But it isn't the whole story — pure Bernoulli arguments mislead about the size of the effect.

A spinning ball drags air along with it, deflecting the airstream. The reaction force is the Magnus force — what makes a curveball curve and a topspin tennis shot dive.

concepts.title: Viscosity
concepts.contentHtml:
Viscosity is a fluid's resistance to shear. Honey is high-viscosity; air is low. Quantitatively, the shear stress equals viscosity times the velocity gradient: τ = μ ∂v/∂y.

Water at 20 °C has μ ≈ 10⁻³ Pa·s. Air, about 50 times less. Honey, about 10⁴ times more.

No real fluid is viscosity-free. The 'inviscid flow' picture is a useful idealization, but the boundary layer near a surface is where viscosity always matters.

concepts.title: Boundary Layers
concepts.contentHtml:
At the surface of a solid, fluid velocity must equal the surface velocity (the no-slip condition). A thin region near the surface — the boundary layer — has steep velocity gradients and viscous effects.

Outside the boundary layer, flow can be approximated as inviscid. This separation is what makes the equations of fluid dynamics tractable.

Boundary layers can be laminar or turbulent. They can also separate from a surface, leading to dramatic increases in drag — what causes a ball to suddenly slow down or a stalled airplane to lose lift.

concepts.title: Reynolds Number
concepts.contentHtml:
The Reynolds number Re = ρvL/μ is the ratio of inertial to viscous forces. It's the single most important dimensionless number in fluid dynamics.

Low Re (≪ 1): viscous, syrupy, predictable laminar flow. A bacterium swimming in water lives at Re ~ 10⁻⁵ — to it, water is essentially honey.

High Re (≫ 1000): inertial dominance, often turbulent. A jetliner at cruise sees Re ~ 10⁸. The transition between laminar and turbulent flow happens around Re ~ 2300 in pipe flow.

title: The Navier-Stokes Equations
description: The unsolved equations that govern most flows

concepts.title: Momentum Conservation in a Fluid
concepts.contentHtml:
Newton's second law for a fluid element gives the Navier-Stokes equation:

ρ(∂v/∂t + v·∇v) = -∇P + μ∇²v + ρg.

Left side: mass times acceleration (with the convective term v·∇v capturing changes felt while moving with the flow). Right: pressure gradients, viscous diffusion, and gravity.

Together with the continuity equation, these are the master equations of fluid dynamics for incompressible flows.

concepts.title: The Million-Dollar Question
concepts.contentHtml:
Do smooth solutions to Navier-Stokes always exist for smooth initial data, or can a finite-time singularity form? Nobody knows.

This is one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems — a million dollars from the Clay Institute for a proof of existence and smoothness, or a counterexample.

The difficulty: the nonlinear convective term v·∇v can produce smaller and smaller eddies, energy cascading down without bound. Whether something blows up at finite time is genuinely open.

concepts.title: Computational Fluid Dynamics
concepts.contentHtml:
Even without an analytic solution, we can solve Navier-Stokes numerically. Discretize space and time, march forward.

CFD designs aircraft wings, predicts weather, simulates blood flow, and optimizes engines. The cost grows steeply with Reynolds number — direct numerical simulation of a jet engine is still infeasible.

Turbulence models (RANS, LES) approximate the smallest-scale eddies cheaply, trading accuracy for tractability.

concepts.title: From Laminar to Turbulent
concepts.contentHtml:
At low Reynolds number, flow is laminar — smooth, predictable, time-reversible. Increase the Reynolds number and instabilities grow; at high enough Re, the flow becomes turbulent: chaotic, three-dimensional, full of swirling eddies at every scale.

You can see this in a smoke trail. Smooth and rope-like for a while, then suddenly bursting into a roiling cloud.

concepts.title: Kolmogorov's Cascade
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1941, Kolmogorov proposed that energy entering turbulence at large scales cascades down to smaller and smaller scales until it dissipates as heat at the smallest (Kolmogorov) scale.

In the inertial range between, the energy spectrum scales as E(k) ∝ k^(-5/3). This 'Kolmogorov spectrum' has been verified in countless experiments — one of the few rigorous results in turbulence.

The total range of scales is set by Re: turbulent eddies span Re^(3/4) decades of length.

concepts.title: Why Turbulence Is Hard
concepts.contentHtml:
Turbulence is deterministic chaos at infinite-dimensional scale. Tiny differences in initial conditions blow up exponentially. Predicting the detailed flow is hopeless; statistics is the best we can do.

The closure problem haunts every attempt to derive equations for averaged quantities — these always involve higher moments, and you can't terminate the chain.

Feynman called turbulence 'the most important unsolved problem of classical physics.' That assessment still stands.
